history.heading: Temasek and British Singapore
paragraphs: Singapore, an island city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, was a trading port known as Temasek in the 14th century and part of the Malay world. It declined after the 15th century.

In 1819 Sir Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company established a trading post, which grew rapidly as a free port. Singapore became part of the Straits Settlements and a key British naval base, attracting immigrants from China, India and the Malay Archipelago. Japan captured Singapore in 1942, a major British defeat, and occupied it until 1945.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Singapore gained self-government in 1959 under Lee Kuan Yew and the People's Action Party (PAP). It joined Malaysia in 1963 but was expelled in 1965 after political and ethnic tensions, becoming an independent republic on 9 August 1965.

Under Lee Kuan Yew, prime minister until 1990, Singapore transformed from a poor port with few resources into one of the richest countries in the world. Lee Hsien Loong led from 2004 to 2024, succeeded by Lawrence Wong.

culture.heading: A multiracial society
paragraphs: Singapore's population is mainly Chinese, Malay and Indian. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are official languages, with English the common working language; Singlish is a local creole. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, Taoism and Hinduism are all practised, and religious harmony is actively promoted.
Hawker centres, serving dishes such as Hainanese chicken rice, laksa, chilli crab and roti prata, are recognised by UNESCO. Landmarks include Marina Bay Sands and Gardens by the Bay.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Singapore is a parliamentary republic. The PAP has won every election since 1959, though the opposition Workers' Party has gained seats. The government is known for efficiency and low corruption, but critics point to limits on free speech, media and protest. Singapore maintains good relations with both the United States and China.

economy.heading: A global hub
paragraphs: Singapore has one of the highest GDPs per person in the world. It is a global hub for finance, trade, shipping (one of the world's busiest ports) and aviation (Changi Airport). Manufacturing of semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and petrochemicals is significant.

The government plays a strong role through state investment companies such as Temasek and GIC. Most residents live in public housing, which is largely owned by its occupants. The currency is the Singapore dollar.
